title: Die kluge Bauerntochter
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 94. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 94, one of the collection’s clearest riddle-tales. A poor farmer’s daughter warns her father that giving the king a found golden mortar without its pestle will only get him asked for the pestle too — and she is proved right: he lands in prison until she is fetched to answer the king’s own riddle, to come to him “not clothed and not naked, not riding and not driving, not on the road and not off it,” which she solves with a fishing net, a donkey, and her own big toe, and is married for her wit. Years later, as queen, she cannot resist quietly fixing an unjust royal judgment over a foal born among a stranger’s oxen, and is sent home in disgrace — allowed to take only “the dearest and best” she knows, which of course turns out to be her sleeping husband.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein armer Bauer, der hatte kein Land, nur ein kleines Häuschen und eine alleinige Tochter, da sprach die Tochter „wir sollten den Herrn König um ein Stückchen Rottland bitten.“
sentences.l: There was once a poor farmer, he had no land, only a little house and one only daughter, then said the daughter “we ought to ask the lord King for a little piece of clearing-land.”
sentences.i: There was once a poor farmer who had no land, only a small cottage and a single daughter; and the daughter said: “We ought to ask our lord the King for a little piece of newly cleared land.”
sentences.n: “Es war einmal” is the standing opening of these tales — there was once. “der hatte kein Land” carries the sentence on with a demonstrative der where English wants a relative who; the Grimms string clauses together that way throughout. eine alleinige Tochter is an only daughter, alleinig where modern German says einzig. Rottland, from roden, to clear, is ground newly grubbed out of waste or wood — the poorest land there is to give away.

sentences.t: Da der König ihre Armuth hörte, schenkte er ihnen auch ein Eckchen Rasen, den hackte sie und ihr Vater um, und wollten ein wenig Korn und der Art Frucht darauf säen.
sentences.l: As the King heard of their poverty, he gave them indeed a little corner of turf, that she and her father hoed over, and wanted to sow a little corn and crop of that kind on it.
sentences.i: When the King heard how poor they were, he did give them a little corner of grassland, and she and her father broke it up with the hoe, meaning to sow a little corn and crops of that sort on it.
sentences.n: Da here is “when, since,” not “there.” Armuth is the 1857 spelling of Armut; the th of Armuth, Rath, Noth drops out of German later. umhacken is separable — “den hackte sie … um,” they hoed it over, turned the sod. “der Art Frucht” is a genitive of description, crop of that kind; Frucht in the older farming sense is the standing crop, not fruit on a tree.

sentences.t: Als sie den Acker beinah herum hatten, so fanden sie in der Erde einen Mörsel von purem Gold.
sentences.l: When they had the field nearly round, so found they in the earth a mortar of pure gold.
sentences.i: When they had almost worked their way round the field, they found in the earth a mortar of pure gold.
sentences.n: “den Acker herum haben” is farming talk — to have got round the whole plot. The so before the main clause is the old resumptive “then,” which German still allowed after a subordinate clause. Ein Mörsel is the mortar, the vessel; its pestle, der Stößer, is the thing that will be missing.

sentences.t: „Hör,“ sagte der Vater zu dem Mädchen, „weil unser Herr König ist so gnädig gewesen und hat uns diesen Acker geschenkt, so müssen wir ihm den Mörsel dafür geben.“
sentences.l: “Listen,” said the father to the girl, “because our lord King has been so gracious and has given us this field, so must we give him the mortar for it.”
sentences.i: “Listen,” said the father to the girl, “since our lord the King has been so gracious and given us this field, we must give him the mortar in return.”
sentences.n: Hör is the bare imperative of hören, used as “listen here.” In careful writing weil sends its verb to the end; here the father speaks as people speak — “weil unser Herr König ist so gnädig gewesen” — with the verb left in second place. dafür is for that, in exchange for it.

sentences.t: Die Tochter aber wollt es nicht bewilligen und sagte „Vater, wenn wir den Mörsel haben und haben den Stößer nicht, dann müssen wir auch den Stößer herbei schaffen, darum schweigt lieber still.“
sentences.l: The daughter however would not allow it and said “Father, if we have the mortar and have not the pestle, then must we produce the pestle as well, therefore keep rather quiet.”
sentences.i: But the daughter would not agree to it, and said: “Father, if we have the mortar and have not the pestle, then we shall have to produce the pestle too; so you had better hold your peace.”
sentences.n: wollt is the clipped wollte. herbei schaffen — printed apart here and as one word a few lines later — is to get a thing brought to the spot, to produce it. She addresses her father with the plural schweigt, the respectful form a child used to a parent.

sentences.t: Er wollte ihr aber nicht gehorchen, nahm den Mörsel, trug ihn zum Herrn König und sagte den hätte er gefunden in der Heide, ob er ihn als eine Verehrung annehmen wollte.
sentences.l: He would not obey her however, took the mortar, carried it to the lord King and said he had found it in the heath, whether he would accept it as a gift of honour.
sentences.i: But he would not listen to her; he took the mortar, carried it to the King, and said he had found it out on the heath, and would he accept it as a gift of honour.
sentences.n: gehorchen takes the dative — ihr, obey her. “sagte den hätte er gefunden” is reported speech with no daß: the subjunctive hätte alone marks the words as the farmer’s, not the narrator’s. eine Verehrung is a respectful present, a gift offered in honour, not modern veneration.

sentences.t: Der König nahm den Mörsel und fragte ob er nichts mehr gefunden hätte?
sentences.l: The King took the mortar and asked whether he had found nothing more?
sentences.i: The King took the mortar and asked whether he had not found anything else.
sentences.n: The question mark stands although the question is reported and not direct — the 1857 text punctuates by the sound of a sentence rather than by rule.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Bauer.
sentences.l: “No,” answered the farmer.
sentences.n: The whole tale turns on this one word: he denies a pestle he never had, and the denial is what no one will believe.

sentences.t: Da sagte der König er sollte nun auch den Stößer herbeischaffen.
sentences.l: Then said the King he should now produce the pestle as well.
sentences.i: Then the King said he must now produce the pestle too.
sentences.n: Reported speech again with no daß, carried by the past sollte. herbeischaffen is written as one word here and apart three sentences ago; 1857 practice varies from line to line.

sentences.t: Der Bauer sprach den hätten sie nicht gefunden;
sentences.l: The farmer said that one they had not found;
sentences.i: The farmer said they had not found it;
sentences.n: den is the demonstrative pronoun pointing back to the pestle, and it stands first for emphasis: that one they had not found. hätten is once more the subjunctive of reported speech. sprach for “said” runs through all these tales.

sentences.t: aber das half ihm so viel, als hätt ers in den Wind gesagt, er ward ins Gefängnis gesetzt, und sollte so lange da sitzen, bis er den Stößer herbeigeschafft hätte.
sentences.l: but that helped him just as much as if he had said it into the wind, he was set into prison, and should sit there so long until he had produced the pestle.
sentences.i: but that helped him about as much as if he had spoken it to the wind; he was put in prison, and was to sit there until he produced the pestle.
sentences.n: “in den Wind sagen” — to speak to no purpose. hätt ers = hätte er es, with both vowel and pronoun clipped away. ward is the old past of werden, modern wurde, and carries the passive here: he was put in prison.

sentences.t: Die Bedienten mußten ihm täglich Wasser und Brot bringen, was man so in dem Gefängnis kriegt, da hörten sie, wie der Mann als fort schrie „ach, hätt ich meiner Tochter gehört! ach, ach, hätt ich meiner Tochter gehört!“
sentences.l: The servants had to bring him daily water and bread, what one gets so in prison, then they heard how the man cried on and on “ah, had I listened to my daughter! ah, ah, had I listened to my daughter!”
sentences.i: The servants had to bring him water and bread every day, the fare one gets in prison; and they heard the man crying over and over: “Ah, if only I had listened to my daughter! Ah, ah, if only I had listened to my daughter!”
sentences.n: “als fort” is the old “continually, on and on” — als here is not “as” but an adverb of repetition, and fort carries the going-on. “hätt ich … gehört” is a wish with the verb first and no wenn: had I but listened. “auf jemanden hören” is to heed someone, and with the bare dative meiner Tochter it is the same thing.

sentences.t: Da giengen die Bedienten zum König und sprachen das, wie der Gefangene als fort schrie „ach, hätt ich doch meiner Tochter gehört!“
sentences.l: Then went the servants to the King and said that, how the prisoner cried on and on “ah, had I but listened to my daughter!”
sentences.i: Then the servants went to the King and reported it — how the prisoner kept crying: “Ah, if only I had listened to my daughter!”
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging, and gieng, fieng, hieng all keep that ie. “sprachen das” is simply said that, reported the matter. doch inside a wish sharpens the regret to “if only.”

sentences.t: und wollte nicht essen und nicht trinken.
sentences.l: and would not eat and not drink.
sentences.i: and would neither eat nor drink.
sentences.n: The subject is still the prisoner, carried over from the reported clause although the sentence has left his words behind; German lets a run of clauses hold a subject that loosely.

sentences.t: Da befahl er den Bedienten sie sollten den Gefangenen vor ihn bringen, und da fragte ihn der Herr König warum er also fort schrie „ach, hätt ich meiner Tochter gehört!“
sentences.l: Then commanded he the servants they should bring the prisoner before him, and then asked him the lord King why he cried so on and on “ah, had I listened to my daughter!”
sentences.i: Then he ordered the servants to bring the prisoner before him, and the King asked him why he cried out so continually: “Ah, if only I had listened to my daughter!”
sentences.n: befehlen takes the dative of the person commanded, den Bedienten. also here is the older “thus, in that way,” not modern “also.”

sentences.t: „Was hat eure Tochter denn gesagt?“
sentences.l: “What did your daughter say then?”
sentences.n: denn in a question is the little push of impatience — well, what did she say? eure is the plural “your,” the King addressing the farmer as ihr.

sentences.t: „Ja sie hat gesprochen ich sollte den Mörsel nicht bringen, sonst müßt ich auch den Stößer schaffen.“
sentences.l: “Yes she has said I should not bring the mortar, otherwise must I produce the pestle as well.”
sentences.i: “Why, she said I ought not to bring the mortar, or else I should have to produce the pestle too.”
sentences.n: Ja opening a sentence is not “yes” but the particle — why, well. müßt is the clipped subjunctive müßte, with the 1857 ß where modern German writes ss.

sentences.t: „Habt ihr so eine kluge Tochter, so laßt sie einmal herkommen.“
sentences.l: “Have you so clever a daughter, then let her come here once.”
sentences.i: “If you have so clever a daughter, let her come here.”
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: the verb first, “Habt ihr …,” does the work of “if you have.” einmal is the softening “just” of a command, not “once.”

sentences.t: Also mußte sie vor den König kommen, der fragte sie ob sie denn so klug wäre, und sagte er wollte ihr ein Räthsel aufgeben, wenn sie das treffen könnte, dann wollte er sie heirathen.
sentences.l: So had she to come before the King, he asked her whether she were then so clever, and said he would set her a riddle, if she could hit it, then would he marry her.
sentences.i: So she had to come before the King, who asked whether she was really so clever, and said he would set her a riddle, and if she could guess it, then he would marry her.
sentences.n: Räthsel and heirathen keep the 1857 th (modern Rätsel, heiraten). “ein Räthsel aufgeben” is to set a riddle; treffen, literally to hit, is the old word for guessing one right.

sentences.t: Da sprach sie gleich ja, sie wollts errathen.
sentences.l: Then said she at once yes, she would guess it.
sentences.i: She said yes at once, she would guess it.
sentences.n: wollts = wollte es. errathen, modern erraten, is to guess a thing out; the er- prefix carries the getting-there.

sentences.t: Da sagte der König „komm zu mir, nicht gekleidet, nicht nackend, nicht geritten, nicht gefahren, nicht in dem Weg, nicht außer dem Weg, und wenn du das kannst, will ich dich heirathen.“
sentences.l: Then said the King “come to me, not clothed, not naked, not ridden, not driven, not in the road, not off the road, and if you can do that, I will marry you.”
sentences.i: Then the King said: “Come to me not clothed and not naked, not riding and not driving, not in the road and not off the road; and if you can do that, I will marry you.”
sentences.n: The riddle is built of past participles standing as bare adjectives — geritten, gefahren describe how she arrives, on horseback or in a vehicle. nackend is the older nackt. Each pair shuts a door, and she must find the crack between them.

sentences.t: Da gieng sie hin, und zog sich aus splinternackend, da war sie nicht gekleidet, und nahm ein großes Fischgarn, und setzte sich hinein und wickelte es ganz um sich herum, da war sie nicht nackend:
sentences.l: Then went she off, and undressed herself stark naked, so was she not clothed, and took a great fishing-net, and set herself into it and wound it quite round about herself, so was she not naked:
sentences.i: So off she went and stripped herself stark naked — so she was not clothed; and she took a great fishing net and got inside it and wound it all round herself — so she was not naked.
sentences.n: sich ausziehen is separable — “zog sich aus,” took her clothes off. splinternackend is stark naked, modern splitternackt. The colon at the end binds this half of the trick to the next; the whole solution is told in one breath.

sentences.t: und borgte einen Esel fürs Geld und band dem Esel das Fischgarn an den Schwanz, darin er sie fortschleppen mußte, und war das nicht geritten und nicht gefahren:
sentences.l: and borrowed a donkey for money and bound the fishing-net to the donkey’s tail, in which he had to drag her away, and that was not ridden and not driven:
sentences.i: and she hired a donkey for money and tied the fishing net to the donkey’s tail, in which it had to drag her along — and that was not riding and not driving.
sentences.n: borgen is to borrow, and “fürs Geld” makes it a hiring. “band dem Esel … an den Schwanz” is the dative of possession: German names the owner in the dative rather than saying “the donkey’s tail.” darin = worin, in which.

sentences.t: der Esel mußte sie aber in der Fahrgleise schleppen, so daß sie nur mit der großen Zehe auf die Erde kam, und war das nicht in dem Weg und nicht außer dem Wege.
sentences.l: the donkey however had to drag her in the wheel-rut, so that she came onto the earth only with the big toe, and that was not in the road and not off the road.
sentences.i: But the donkey had to drag her along in the wheel rut, so that she touched the ground only with her big toe — and that was neither in the road nor out of it.
sentences.n: die Fahrgleise is the track a cart’s wheels cut into a road; lying in the rut she is below the road’s surface, and touching it with one toe she is not off it either. Wege carries the old dative -e, which 1857 still writes.

sentences.t: Und wie sie so daher kam, sagte der König sie hätte das Räthsel getroffen, und es wäre alles erfüllt.
sentences.l: And when she came along in that way, said the King she had hit the riddle, and everything was fulfilled.
sentences.i: And when she came along like that, the King said she had guessed the riddle and had fulfilled it all.
sentences.n: daherkommen is to come along, to arrive in view. hätte and wäre are the subjunctive of reported speech again — the King’s verdict in his own words.

sentences.t: Da ließ er ihren Vater los aus dem Gefängnis, und nahm sie bei sich als seine Gemahlin und befahl ihr das ganze königliche Gut an.
sentences.l: Then let he her father loose out of the prison, and took her to himself as his consort and committed to her the whole royal property.
sentences.i: Then he let her father out of prison, took her to himself as his wife, and put the whole royal estate into her hands.
sentences.n: loslassen and anbefehlen are both separable and both stand split — “ließ … los,” “befahl … an.” anbefehlen is to entrust a thing to someone; Gemahlin is the elevated word for wife, the one used of a queen.

sentences.t: Nun waren etliche Jahre herum, als der Herr König einmal auf die Parade zog, da trug es sich zu, daß Bauern mit ihren Wagen vor dem Schloß hielten, die hatten Holz verkauft;
sentences.l: Now were some years round, when the lord King once went out to the parade, then it came about that farmers with their wagons halted before the castle, they had sold wood;
sentences.i: Now some years had gone round, and once when the King rode out to the parade it happened that farmers halted with their wagons before the castle; they had been selling wood.
sentences.n: “die Jahre sind herum” — the years are up, gone round. “es trug sich zu,” from sich zutragen, is the old impersonal for “it came to pass.” die Parade is the review of troops, and the King is riding out to it.

sentences.t: etliche hatten Ochsen vorgespannt, und etliche Pferde.
sentences.l: some had oxen harnessed in front, and some horses.
sentences.i: some had oxen in the traces, and some horses.
sentences.n: vorspannen is to hitch an animal in front of a cart. etliche is the older “some, several,” now largely gone out of ordinary speech.

sentences.t: Da war ein Bauer, der hatte drei Pferde, davon kriegte eins ein junges Füllchen, das lief weg und legte sich mitten zwischen zwei Ochsen, die vor dem Wagen waren.
sentences.l: There was a farmer, he had three horses, of them one got a young little foal, that ran away and laid itself down in the middle between two oxen, which were before the wagon.
sentences.i: There was one farmer who had three horses, and one of them had a young foal, which ran off and lay down between two oxen that were harnessed to a wagon.
sentences.n: “ein Füllen kriegen” is said of the mare — to have a foal. Füllchen is the diminutive, with the -chen ending that makes anything small and dear, and the tale keeps to it. das lief weg takes the neuter relative, because Füllchen is neuter whatever the animal’s sex.

sentences.t: Als nun die Bauern zusammen kamen, fiengen sie an sich zu zanken, zu schmeißen und zu lärmen, und der Ochsenbauer wollte das Füllchen behalten und sagte die Ochsen hättens gehabt:
sentences.l: When now the farmers came together, they began to quarrel, to strike and to make an uproar, and the ox-farmer wanted to keep the little foal and said the oxen had had it:
sentences.i: When the farmers came together they fell to quarrelling, hitting and shouting; and the ox-farmer wanted to keep the foal, and said the oxen had had it.
sentences.n: anfangen is separable — “fiengen sie an … zu zanken”; fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing. schmeißen here is to hit out, to throw blows, not the modern “to fling.” hättens = hätten es, the subjunctive of reported speech.

sentences.t: und der andere sagte nein, seine Pferde hättens gehabt, und es wäre sein.
sentences.l: and the other said no, his horses had had it, and it was his.
sentences.n: sein at the end is the possessive “his,” not the verb — the one German word does duty for both, and only the sentence says which.

sentences.t: Der Zank kam vor den König, und der that den Ausspruch wo das Füllen gelegen hätte, da sollt es bleiben;
sentences.l: The quarrel came before the King, and he gave the pronouncement where the foal had lain, there should it stay;
sentences.i: The quarrel came before the King, and he gave judgment: where the foal had lain, there it should stay.
sentences.n: that is the 1857 spelling of tat (thun and that for tun and tat). “einen Ausspruch thun” is to hand down a ruling. der at the head of the clause is the demonstrative “and he,” pointing back to the King.

sentences.t: und also bekams der Ochsenbauer, dems doch nicht gehörte.
sentences.l: and so got it the ox-farmer, to whom for all that it did not belong.
sentences.i: and so the ox-farmer got it, though it was not his.
sentences.n: bekams = bekam es, dems = dem es; 1857 prints these clipped forms without an apostrophe. gehören takes the dative of the owner. doch here is the concessive “and yet.”

sentences.t: Da gieng der andere weg, weinte und lamentierte über sein Füllchen.
sentences.l: Then went the other away, wept and lamented over his little foal.
sentences.i: Then the other went away, weeping and lamenting over his foal.
sentences.n: lamentieren, from the Latin, is to wail aloud and go on about it — a shade broader than “to lament.”

sentences.t: Nun hatte er gehört wie daß die Frau Königin so gnädig wäre, weil sie auch von armen Bauersleuten gekommen wäre:
sentences.l: Now had he heard how that the lady Queen was so gracious, because she too had come of poor farming folk:
sentences.i: Now he had heard how the Queen was so gracious, because she too had come of poor farming people.
sentences.n: “wie daß” is an old doubled conjunction, how that, where either word alone would do. Bauersleute are country people, the folk of a farm. Both verbs stand in the subjunctive because this is what he had heard, not what the tale asserts.

sentences.t: gieng er zu ihr und bat sie ob sie ihm nicht helfen könnte daß er sein Füllchen wieder bekäme.
sentences.l: went he to her and asked her whether she could not help him that he might get his little foal again.
sentences.i: So he went to her and asked whether she could not help him to get his foal back.
sentences.n: bitten with a bare ob-clause is the older construction, to ask whether. helfen takes the dative, ihm. “daß … bekäme” is a purpose clause in the subjunctive, so that he might get it back.

sentences.t: Sagte sie „ja, wenn ihr mir versprecht daß ihr mich nicht verrathen wollt, so will ichs euch sagen.
sentences.l: Said she “yes, if you promise me that you will not betray me, then will I tell it you.
sentences.i: She said: “Yes — if you promise me you will not give me away, I will tell you.
sentences.n: The verb-first “Sagte sie” for “she said” is a narrative habit of this tale and comes several times over. She addresses him with the plural ihr, the ordinary polite form of the time. verrathen is the 1857 verraten, to give away, betray.

sentences.t: Morgen früh, wenn der König auf der Wachtparade ist, so stellt euch hin mitten in die Straße, wo er vorbei kommen muß, nehmt ein großes Fischgarn und thut als fischtet ihr, und fischt also fort und schüttet das Garn aus, als wenn ihrs voll hättet,“ und sagte ihm auch was er antworten sollte, wenn er vom König gefragt würde.
sentences.l: Tomorrow early, when the King is at the guard-parade, then place yourself in the middle of the street, where he must come past, take a great fishing-net and act as if you were fishing, and go on fishing so and shake the net out, as if you had it full,” and told him also what he should answer, if he were asked by the King.
sentences.i: Tomorrow morning, when the King is at the guard parade, plant yourself in the middle of the street where he must pass, take a great fishing net and make as if you were fishing, and keep fishing away and shake out the net as if you had it full” — and she told him too what he was to answer when the King questioned him.
sentences.n: sich hinstellen is separable — “stellt euch hin,” post yourself. “thut als fischtet ihr” uses the bare past subjunctive after als, with no wenn, for a pretended action. “fischt also fort” is go on fishing in that way, with fort carrying the keeping-on, as it did in the prisoner’s “als fort schrie.”

sentences.t: Also stand der Bauer am andern Tag da und fischte auf einem trockenen Platz.
sentences.l: So stood the farmer the next day there and fished on a dry place.
sentences.i: So the next day the farmer stood there fishing on a dry patch of ground.
sentences.n: “am andern Tag” is the next day, ander in its old sense of second, following.

sentences.t: Wie der König vorbei kam und das sah, schickte er seinen Laufer hin, der sollte fragen was der närrische Mann vor hätte.
sentences.l: When the King came past and saw that, sent he his runner over, he should ask what the foolish man had in mind.
sentences.i: When the King came by and saw it, he sent his runner over to ask what the foolish fellow was about.
sentences.n: Ein Laufer, modern Läufer, was a servant kept to run errands and go before his master. “was er vor hätte” is vorhaben, separable, to have a thing in view, to be up to something. närrisch is fool’s behaviour, from der Narr.

sentences.t: Da gab er zur Antwort „ich fische.“
sentences.l: Then gave he as answer “I am fishing.”
sentences.i: He answered: “I am fishing.”
sentences.n: German has one present tense where English has two — “ich fische” is I fish and I am fishing alike, and here it can only be the second.

sentences.t: Fragte der Laufer wie er fischen könnte, es wäre ja kein Wasser da.
sentences.l: Asked the runner how he could fish, there was after all no water there.
sentences.i: The runner asked how he could be fishing — there was no water there at all.
sentences.n: ja is the particle, not “yes”: it appeals to what both men can see. Both verbs are subjunctive because the runner’s words are reported.

sentences.t: Sagte der Bauer „so gut als zwei Ochsen können ein Füllen kriegen, so gut kann ich auch auf dem trockenen Platz fischen.“
sentences.l: Said the farmer “as well as two oxen can have a foal, so well can I also fish on the dry place.”
sentences.i: The farmer said: “Just as well as two oxen can have a foal, just so well can I fish on dry ground.”
sentences.n: “so gut als … so gut” is the old correlative pair, as … so; modern German would say so gut wie. The whole answer is the Queen’s, given him word for word the evening before.

sentences.t: Der Laufer gieng hin und brachte dem König die Antwort, da ließ er den Bauer vor sich kommen und sagte ihm das hätte er nicht von sich, von wem er das hätte:
sentences.l: The runner went over and brought the King the answer, then let he the farmer come before him and said to him he had not that of himself, from whom he had it:
sentences.i: The runner went and brought the King the answer; then the King had the farmer brought before him and told him he had not got that out of his own head — from whom did he have it?
sentences.n: “etwas von sich haben” is to have a thing of oneself, out of one’s own head. The King’s question is folded into the reported speech without a question mark, and the colon carries it into the next clause.

sentences.t: und sollts gleich bekennen.
sentences.l: and he should confess it at once.
sentences.i: and he was to own up at once.
sentences.n: sollts = sollte es. bekennen is to admit, to own up to; the subject is still the farmer, carried over from the sentence before.

sentences.t: Der Bauer aber wollts nicht thun und sagte immer Gott bewahr! er hätt es von sich.
sentences.l: The farmer however would not do it and said always God preserve us! he had it of himself.
sentences.i: But the farmer would not do it, and kept saying: God forbid! he had it of himself.
sentences.n: thun is the 1857 tun. “Gott bewahr!” — God preserve us — is the everyday cry of denial. immer here is over and over: he kept saying it.

sentences.t: Sie legten ihn aber auf ein Gebund Stroh und schlugen und drangsalten ihn so lange, bis ers bekannte, daß ers von der Frau Königin hätte.
sentences.l: They laid him however on a bundle of straw and struck and tormented him so long, until he confessed it, that he had it from the lady Queen.
sentences.i: But they laid him on a truss of straw and beat and tormented him until he confessed that he had it from the Queen.
sentences.n: Ein Gebund Stroh is a bound truss of straw, and laying a man out on it is the preparation for a beating. drangsalen, modern drangsalieren, is to harry, to torment. The tale does not soften what is done to him.

sentences.t: Als der König nach Haus kam, sagte er zu seiner Frau „warum bist du so falsch mit mir, ich will dich nicht mehr zur Gemahlin:
sentences.l: When the King came home, he said to his wife “why are you so false with me, I will not have you for consort any more:
sentences.i: When the King came home he said to his wife: “Why are you so false with me? I will have you for my wife no longer.
sentences.n: “zur Gemahlin wollen” is to want someone for a wife; zu with the dative names what a person is taken as. falsch of a person is treacherous, double-dealing. He turns her out with the intimate du, as they have always spoken.

sentences.t: deine Zeit ist um, geh wieder hin, woher du kommen bist, in dein Bauernhäuschen.“
sentences.l: your time is up, go back again, from where you have come, into your little farmhouse.”
sentences.i: your time is up; go back where you came from, to your little farmhouse.”
sentences.n: “die Zeit ist um” — the time is up, run out. “woher du kommen bist” — older German builds the perfect of kommen with sein and lets the participle stand before it.

sentences.t: Doch erlaubte er ihr eins, sie sollte sich das Liebste und Beste mitnehmen was sie wüßte, und das sollte ihr Abschied sein.
sentences.l: Yet allowed he her one thing, she should take with her the dearest and best that she knew, and that should be her leave-taking.
sentences.i: Yet he allowed her one thing: she was to take with her the dearest and best she knew of, and that should be her parting gift.
sentences.n: das Liebste und Beste are adjectives used as neuter nouns — the dearest and best thing there is. mitnehmen is separable. Abschied is both the leave-taking and what one carries away from it; the King means a parting present, and it will be turned against him.

sentences.t: Sie sagte „ja, lieber Mann, wenn dus so befiehlst, will ich es auch thun,“ und fiel über ihn her und küßte ihn und sprach sie wollte Abschied von ihm nehmen.
sentences.l: She said “yes, dear husband, if you command it so, will I do it too,” and fell upon him and kissed him and said she wanted to take leave of him.
sentences.i: She said: “Yes, dear husband, if that is your command, I will do it,” and she fell upon him and kissed him and said she would take her leave of him.
sentences.n: Mann is husband here, as Frau is wife. dus = du es. “über jemanden herfallen” is to fall upon someone — used of an attack elsewhere and warm here, which is part of the joke.

sentences.t: Dann ließ sie einen starken Schlaftrunk kommen, Abschied mit ihm zu trinken:
sentences.l: Then had she a strong sleeping-draught brought, to drink a farewell with him:
sentences.i: Then she had a strong sleeping draught brought, to drink a farewell with him.
sentences.n: “kommen lassen” is to send for a thing, to have it fetched. Ein Schlaftrunk is a drink to make one sleep; the compound says just what it does.

sentences.t: der König that einen großen Zug, sie aber trank nur ein wenig.
sentences.l: the King did a great draught, she however drank only a little.
sentences.i: The King took a great pull at it, but she drank only a little.
sentences.n: “einen Zug thun” is to take a pull, a swallow, from ziehen — the same word as a draught of air.

sentences.t: Da gerieth er bald in einen tiefen Schlaf und als sie das sah, rief sie einen Bedienten und nahm ein schönes weißes Linnentuch und schlug ihn da hinein, und die Bedienten mußten ihn in einen Wagen vor die Thüre tragen, und fuhr sie ihn heim in ihr Häuschen.
sentences.l: Then fell he soon into a deep sleep and when she saw that, called she a servant and took a fine white linen cloth and wrapped him into it, and the servants had to carry him into a wagon before the door, and drove she him home into her little house.
sentences.i: He soon fell into a deep sleep; and when she saw it she called a servant, took a fine white linen sheet and wrapped him up in it, and the servants had to carry him out to a wagon at the door, and she drove him home to her cottage.
sentences.n: gerathen, modern geraten, is to come into a state, here to fall asleep. “schlug ihn da hinein” is einschlagen, to wrap a thing up in cloth. Linnentuch is the older Leinentuch, linen. The last clause slips into verb-first — “und fuhr sie ihn heim” — as the tale hurries to the end of the night.

sentences.t: Da legte sie ihn in ihr Bettchen, und er schlief Tag und Nacht in einem fort, und als er aufwachte, sah er sich um, und sagte „ach Gott, wo bin ich denn?“
sentences.l: Then laid she him in her little bed, and he slept day and night on end, and when he awoke, looked he about him, and said “ah God, where am I then?”
sentences.i: There she laid him in her little bed, and he slept day and night on end; and when he awoke he looked about him and said: “Ah God, where am I?”
sentences.n: “in einem fort” — on and on without a break. sich umsehen is separable and reflexive, to look about oneself.

sentences.t: rief seinen Bedienten, aber es war keiner da.
sentences.l: called his servant, but there was none there.
sentences.i: He called his servant, but there was none there.
sentences.n: The subject he is left out altogether, as German allows when the same subject carries on from the sentence before.

sentences.t: Endlich kam seine Frau vors Bett und sagte „lieber Herr König, ihr habt mir befohlen ich sollte das Liebste und Beste aus dem Schloß mitnehmen, nun hab ich nichts Besseres und Lieberes als dich, da hab ich dich mitgenommen.“
sentences.l: At last came his wife before the bed and said “dear lord King, you have commanded me I should take the dearest and best out of the castle, now have I nothing better and dearer than you, so have I taken you with me.”
sentences.i: At last his wife came to the bedside and said: “Dear lord King, you commanded me to take the dearest and best out of the castle; now I have nothing better and dearer than you, so I have taken you.”
sentences.n: She addresses him with the respectful plural ihr and then, in the same breath, with the intimate dich — the form changes as the argument turns from the King to the man. Besseres and Lieberes are the comparatives of the King’s own neuter nouns, so that his words come back at him.

sentences.t: Dem König stiegen die Thränen in die Augen, und er sagte „liebe Frau, du sollst mein sein und ich dein,“ und nahm sie wieder mit ins königliche Schloß und ließ sich aufs neue mit ihr vermählen;
sentences.l: To the King the tears rose into the eyes, and he said “dear wife, you shall be mine and I yours,” and took her again with him into the royal castle and had himself wedded to her anew;
sentences.i: The tears rose in the King’s eyes, and he said: “Dear wife, you shall be mine and I yours,” and he took her back with him to the royal castle and had himself married to her afresh.
sentences.n: “Dem König stiegen die Thränen in die Augen” is the dative of possession: German names the person in the dative and leaves the eyes a plain article. Thränen keeps the 1857 th (modern Tränen). sich vermählen is the elevated word for marrying.

sentences.t: und werden sie ja wohl noch auf den heutigen Tag leben.
sentences.l: and they will surely be living still on the present day.
sentences.i: and they are surely living to this very day.
sentences.n: The closing formula. ja wohl together are not “yes indeed” but a shrug of assurance — surely, no doubt; and the German future werden … leben leaves them alive as the tale ends.

glossary.abschied: der Abschied — farewell, leave-taking; here also the parting gift (noun, m.)
glossary.annehmen: annehmen — to accept, to receive (infinitive; separable an-)
glossary.aufgeben: aufgeben — to set, to pose (a riddle) (infinitive; ein Räthsel aufgeben)
glossary.band: binden — bound, tied (3rd sg. past; band … an den Schwanz, tied to the tail — not das Band)
glossary.bekannte: bekennen — confessed, owned up (3rd sg. past; not der Bekannte, acquaintance)
glossary.bewahr: bewahren — preserve (in „Gott bewahr!“, God forbid! — old optative subjunctive, modern bewahre)
glossary.bitten: bitten — to ask (for), to beg (infinitive; um etwas bitten)
glossary.denn: denn — (particle in questions) then, well (was hat sie denn gesagt?)
glossary.eckchen: das Eckchen — little corner, small patch (diminutive of die Ecke; ein Eckchen Rasen)
glossary.eins: eins — one thing; one of them (neuter pronoun)
glossary.es: es — it; also the impersonal es (es war einmal; es trug sich zu)
glossary.fische: fischen — (I) fish, am fishing (1st sg. present; not der Fisch)
glossary.fort: fort — on, continually (als fort schrie: kept crying; fischt also fort: keep on fishing)
glossary.fragen: fragen — to ask (infinitive; not die Frage)
glossary.fuhr: fahren — drove, carried (3rd sg. past; fuhr sie ihn heim, she drove him home)
glossary.füllen: das Füllen — foal (neuter noun; not the verb füllen, to fill)
glossary.garn: das Garn — net, the fishing net (lit. yarn, twine)
glossary.gefangene: der Gefangene — the prisoner (adjectival noun, nom. sg.)
glossary.gesetzt: setzen — put, placed (past part.; ins Gefängnis gesetzt werden, to be put in prison)
glossary.getroffen: treffen — guessed right, hit upon (past part.; ein Räthsel treffen)
glossary.gut: gut — good, well; das Gut — property, estate (das königliche Gut)
glossary.hab: haben — (I) have (1st sg. present, clipped habe)
glossary.hackte: umhacken — hoed over, broke up the sod (3rd sg. past; separable: hackte … um)
glossary.ja: ja — yes; also the particle: after all, you see
glossary.junges: jung — young (adj., inflected neuter; ein junges Füllchen)
glossary.leben: leben — to live (infinitive; not das Leben)
glossary.lieber: lieber — rather, better (adv.; schweigt lieber still); also lieb, dear (inflected)
glossary.los: loslassen — let loose, released (separable: ließ … los)
glossary.lärmen: lärmen — to make a din, to be noisy (infinitive)
glossary.morgen: morgen — tomorrow (adv.; Morgen früh, tomorrow morning)
glossary.purem: pur — pure (adj., dat. sg.; von purem Gold, of pure gold)
glossary.schlaf: der Schlaf — sleep (noun, m.; in einen tiefen Schlaf)
glossary.schlug: schlagen — wrapped (schlug ihn da hinein, wrapped him up in it); also struck
glossary.sollt: sollte — should, was to (3rd sg. past, clipped; da sollt es bleiben)
glossary.thut: thun — do! act! (2nd pl. imperative; 1857 spelling of tut)
glossary.treffen: treffen — to guess (a riddle) right (lit. to hit)
glossary.verkauft: verkaufen — sold (past part.; hatten Holz verkauft)
glossary.verrathen: verrathen — to betray, to give away (infinitive; 1857 spelling of verraten)
glossary.ward: werden — was (passive auxiliary: ward gesetzt, was put); became (archaic wurde)
glossary.wege: der Weg — way, road (dat. sg. with the old -e: außer dem Wege)
glossary.wollt: wollen — wanted, would (3rd sg. past, clipped wollte); also 2nd pl. present wollt
glossary.zog: ziehen — rode out (auf die Parade zog); sich ausziehen: undressed (zog sich aus)
